target.statement: The achievement set of the positive series x_n = 1 / (2^n - 1) has Lebesgue measure exactly 1.

nearest_prior_work: Bartoszewicz, Filipczak, and Prus-Wisniowski (2013), Theorem 21.10: for a quickly convergent positive series, the achievement-set measure is lim 2^n r_n.
Kovac and Tao (2024), Remarks 12-13: the fixed-base Lambert weights 1/(t^n-1) satisfy the strict-tail condition and consequently have Cantor topology and unique coding.
Bartoszewicz, Glab, and Marchwicki (2018), Example 4.5: an explicit worked use of the same lim 2^n r_n measure formula for another quickly convergent sequence.
classification.attribution: Attribute the general measure formula to the classical achievement-set literature, with the 2013 theorem as the exact modern source anchor. Attribute the Mersenne strict-tail/Cantor premise to Kovac-Tao. Do not attribute the exact measure-one computation to Kovac-Tao.
classification.mathematical_interest: The exact value 1 exhibits a fat, nowhere-dense Cantor set at the base-two boundary. The corresponding fixed-base weights for t >= 3 have measure zero under the same formula, so base two is the sharp measure phase boundary within this family.
classification.reusable_scope: The same two-line squeeze evaluates lim 2^n r_n for asymptotically geometric quickly convergent subsum families; it separates the topological strict-tail input from the quantitative measure computation.
classification.why_it_matters: It corrects an inflated and internally contradictory public-story route without diminishing the result's geometric interest: the Lean theorem is a useful exact formalisation, but not evidence of a new standalone measure theorem.

primary_sources.supports: A primary worked application confirming how the classical limit formula is used; it is not the Mersenne specialisation.

specialisation_proof.notation: Let x_n = 1/(2^n-1) and r_n = sum_{k>n} x_k.
specialisation_proof.strict_tail_source: Kovac-Tao Remark 13 proves x_n > r_n, so Theorem 21.10 applies.
squeeze: Therefore 1 < 2^n r_n <= 1/(1-2^-(n+1)), so 2^n r_n tends to 1.
specialisation_proof.conclusion: Theorem 21.10 gives Lebesgue measure 1. This is a direct specialisation of the general formula, independent of the Lean implementation.
